LICENSE SUSPENSION FOR UNPAID CHILD SUPPORT (FAMILY CODE SECTION 17520) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Taylor Morgan · Jordan Alex Lee

DECLARATION -- SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's child support license suspension and denial program under Family Code Section 17520, which allows a local child support agency to certify a support obligor as out of compliance with a support order to the Department of Child Support Services for referral to state licensing boards, in connection with a matter between Taylor Morgan and Jordan Alex Lee, case number CGC-26-123456, pending in Sacramento County. It describes the statute's definitions of "board," "license," and "compliance with a judgment or order for support," the certified-list and consolidated-list process, the temporary-license and notice provisions, the supplemental list used for suspending an existing license, the no-refund rule, the grounds on which a local child support agency must send a release, the judicial review process and its limited scope, the statute's sole-administrative-remedy provision, and the statute's specific protections for a suspended driver's license against vehicle impoundment and increased insurance costs. It does not itself certify any obligor to any board, request or grant any release, temporary license, suspension, or judicial review, and it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney about how Family Code Section 17520 applies to a specific case.

WHICH BOARDS AND LICENSES THE STATUTE REACHES
Under California law, Family Code Section 17520 defines "board" broadly to include the State Bar of California, the Department of Real Estate, the Department of Motor Vehicles, the Secretary of State, the Department of Fish and Wildlife, and any other state entity that issues a license, certificate, credential, permit, registration, or other authorization to engage in a business, occupation, or profession, or, to the extent required by federal law, for recreational purposes. "License" is defined equally broadly, reaching State Bar membership, a commercial motor vehicle authorization, a notary public commission, a Department of Motor Vehicles driver's license, a Department of Fish and Wildlife commercial fishing license, and, to the extent required by federal law, a recreational-purpose license, in addition to conventional business, occupation, and professional licenses.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Board” means an entity specified in Section 101 of the Business and Professions Code, the entities referred to in Sections 1000 and 3600 of the Business and Professions Code, the State Bar of California, the Department of Real Estate, the Department of Motor Vehicles, the Secretary of State, the Department of Fish and Wildlife, and any other state commission, department, committee, examiner, or agency that issues a license, certificate, credential, permit, registration, or any other authorization to engage in a business, occupation, or profession, or to the extent required by federal law or regulations, for recreational purposes."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (a)(2), definition of "Board" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=17520.)
  "“License” includes membership in the State Bar of California, and a certificate, credential, permit, registration, or any other authorization issued by a board that allows a person to engage in a business, occupation, or profession, or to operate a commercial motor vehicle, including appointment and commission by the Secretary of State as a notary public. “License” also includes any driver’s license issued by the Department of Motor Vehicles, any commercial fishing license issued by the Department of Fish and Wildlife, and to the extent required by federal law or regulations, any license used for recreational purposes."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (a)(5), definition of "License" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=17520.)
  Known gap: This clause states only the statute's own definitions of "board" and "license"; it does not identify which specific board(s) or license(s), if any, are implicated in a given case, and the statute itself notes that failing to specifically name a particular board or license type does not exclude it from these definitions, so the definitions cannot be treated as an exhaustive list.

WHAT "COMPLIANCE WITH A SUPPORT ORDER" MEANS UNDER THIS STATUTE
Under California law, for purposes of Family Code Section 17520, an obligor is in "compliance with a judgment or order for support" if the obligor is no more than 30 calendar days in arrears on current support, is making periodic payments in full on a support arrearage or a public-assistance reimbursement judgment (whether court ordered or by agreement with the local child support agency), or has obtained a judicial finding that equitable estoppel precludes enforcement of the order. The statute further limits its own reach as to spousal support: a local child support agency may use Section 17520 to enforce a spousal support order only when it is also enforcing a related child support obligation owed to the same obligee by the same obligor.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Compliance with a judgment or order for support” means that, as set forth in a judgment or order for child or family support, the obligor is no more than 30 calendar days in arrears in making payments in full for current support, in making periodic payments in full, whether court ordered or by agreement with the local child support agency, on a support arrearage, or in making periodic payments in full, whether court ordered or by agreement with the local child support agency, on a judgment for reimbursement for public assistance, or has obtained a judicial finding that equitable estoppel as provided in statute or case law precludes enforcement of the order. The local child support agency is authorized to use this section to enforce orders for spousal support only when the local child support agency is also enforcing a related child support obligation owed to the obligee parent by the same obligor, pursuant to Sections 17400 and 17604."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (a)(4), definition of "Compliance with a judgment or order for support" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=17520.)
  Known gap: This clause states the statute's own 30-day/periodic-payment compliance definition and its spousal-support limitation; it does not address how "periodic payments in full" is measured against a specific payment schedule, nor does it independently verify the equitable estoppel doctrine referenced by the statute, which the statute describes only as being "provided in statute or case law" without citing a specific source.

THE CERTIFIED LIST AND CONSOLIDATED LIST PROCESS
Under California law, a local child support agency must maintain a list of Title IV-D support obligors against whom a California support order or judgment has been rendered or registered and who are not in compliance with it, and must submit to the Department of Child Support Services a certified list containing each obligor's name, identifying number, and last known address, along with the submitting agency's name, address, and telephone number. The department then consolidates the certified lists received from all local child support agencies and, within 30 calendar days of receipt, provides a copy of the consolidated list to each board responsible for regulating the affected licenses.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The local child support agency shall maintain a list of those persons included in a case being enforced under Title IV-D of the federal Social Security Act against whom a support order or judgment has been rendered by, or registered in, a court of this state, and who are not in compliance with that order or judgment. The local child support agency shall submit a certified list with the names, social security numbers, individual taxpayer identification numbers, or other uniform identification numbers, and last known addresses of these persons and the name, address, and telephone number of the local child support agency who certified the list to the department."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (b), certified list submitted by the local child support agency (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=17520.)
  "The department shall consolidate the certified lists received from the local child support agencies and, within 30 calendar days of receipt, shall provide a copy of the consolidated list to each board that is responsible for the regulation of licenses, as specified in this section."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (c), department's consolidation and distribution to boards (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=17520.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the statutory certification-and-consolidation pipeline as written; it does not state how quickly a local child support agency must add or remove a given obligor's name after a change in compliance status (the statute requires only a monthly updated certified list), and it does not address the accuracy safeguards, if any, that apply before a name reaches a board.

THE 150-DAY TEMPORARY LICENSE FOR A NEW APPLICANT ON THE LIST
Under California law, before issuing or renewing a license, a board must check whether the applicant is on the department's most recent consolidated list, and if the applicant is on the list and is otherwise eligible for a license, the board must issue a temporary license valid for 150 days rather than immediately denying the application. Except for a non-commercial driver's license, that 150-day period generally cannot be extended and only one temporary license may issue per regular license term; for a non-commercial driver's license specifically, the statute allows the board to extend a 150-day temporary license by up to 150 additional days upon a request from the local child support agency or a court order on a showing of good cause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The board shall issue a temporary license valid for a period of 150 days to any applicant whose name is on the certified list if the applicant is otherwise eligible for a license."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (e)(2)(A), 150-day temporary license (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=17520.)
  "This paragraph shall apply only in the case of a driver’s license, other than a commercial driver’s license. Upon the request of the local child support agency or by order of the court upon a showing of good cause, the board shall extend a 150-day temporary license for a period not to exceed 150 extra days."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (e)(2)(D), driver's license extension of the temporary license (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=17520.)
  Known gap: This clause covers the general 150-day temporary-license mechanism and the driver's-license-specific extension; it does not cover the separate supplemental-list suspension process that applies to an obligor who already holds a full license (addressed in a separate clause of this document), and it does not state what happens if the applicant is not otherwise eligible for a license on grounds unrelated to support compliance.

THE SUPPLEMENTAL LIST AND SUSPENSION OF AN EXISTING LICENSE
Under California law, separately from the certified-list/temporary-license process for new applicants, the department may (where economically feasible and where an obligor has been out of compliance for more than four months) provide a supplemental list of these obligors to boards with which it has an interagency agreement, and the licenses of obligors on that supplemental list become subject to suspension, provided the license would not otherwise be up for renewal within six months of the department's request. If a licensee is on a supplemental list, the board must serve notice that the license will be automatically suspended 150 days after notice is served unless compliance with Section 17520 is achieved in the meantime.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The department may, when it is economically feasible for the department and the boards to do so as determined by the department, in cases where the department is aware that certain child support obligors listed on the certified lists have been out of compliance with a judgment or order for support for more than four months, provide a supplemental list of these obligors to each board with which the department has an interagency agreement to implement this paragraph. Upon request by the department, the licenses of these obligors shall be subject to suspension, provided that the licenses would not otherwise be eligible for renewal within six months from the date of the request by the department."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (e)(3)(A), supplemental list and suspension eligibility (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=17520.)
  "If a licensee is on a supplemental list, the board shall immediately serve notice as specified in subdivision (f) on the licensee that the license will be automatically suspended 150 days after notice is served, unless compliance with this section is achieved."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (e)(3)(B), 150-day suspension notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=17520.)
  Known gap: This clause describes the supplemental-list suspension track only as the statute defines it, including its own "economically feasible" and "interagency agreement" preconditions on the department's use of this track; it does not state how a licensee can determine in advance whether their board participates in an interagency agreement under this paragraph, and it excludes licenses subject to annual renewal or annual fee, which the statute places outside this particular paragraph.

NO REFUND OF FEES PAID ON DENIAL OR SUSPENSION
Under California law, if a license, a license application, or a license renewal is denied under Family Code Section 17520, or if a license is suspended under Section 17520, the statute states that any funds already paid by the applicant or licensee to the board are not refunded by the board.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In the event that a license or application for a license or the renewal of a license is denied pursuant to this section, any funds paid by the applicant or licensee shall not be refunded by the board."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (e)(2)(C), no refund on denial (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=17520.)
  Known gap: This clause states only the statute's own no-refund rule; it does not address whether a board's separate fee schedule allows any partial credit toward a future application, which the statute does not address, and it does not state whether this rule differs for a temporary license that lapses versus an application that is denied outright.

WHEN A LOCAL CHILD SUPPORT AGENCY MUST SEND A RELEASE
Under California law, after an applicant makes a timely written request for review, the local child support agency must immediately send a release to the appropriate board and the applicant if the applicant is found to be in compliance, negotiates an arrearage or reimbursement payment schedule with the local child support agency, has requested review but the agency cannot complete it and notify the applicant within the statutory timeframe, has filed and timely pursued judicial review that will not be resolved within 150 days of the notice being served, or has obtained a judicial finding of compliance as the statute defines it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The local child support agency shall immediately send a release to the appropriate board and the applicant, if any of the following conditions are met:(1) The applicant is found to be in compliance or negotiates an agreement with the local child support agency for a payment schedule on arrearages or reimbursement."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (h), release conditions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=17520.)
  Known gap: This clause states the four release-triggering conditions the statute lists; it does not restate the separate cross-referenced timeframe for a local child support agency to resolve a review request (Family Code Section 17800), which this clause does not independently verify, and it does not address what happens if none of the four listed conditions is met.

JUDICIAL REVIEW OF A LOCAL CHILD SUPPORT AGENCY'S DECISION
Under California law, a request for judicial review of a local child support agency's decision must state the grounds for review, and judicial review is limited to those stated grounds; the court must hold an evidentiary hearing within 20 calendar days of the filing of the request. That judicial review is further limited to determining whether a support judgment, order, or payment schedule on arrearages or reimbursement exists, whether the petitioner is the obligor covered by it, and whether the obligor is or is not in compliance with it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The request for judicial review of the local child support agency’s decision shall state the grounds for which review is requested and judicial review shall be limited to those stated grounds. The court shall hold an evidentiary hearing within 20 calendar days of the filing of the request for review."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (k), introductory text on grounds and evidentiary hearing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=17520.)
  "Judicial review of the local child support agency’s decision shall be limited to a determination of each of the following issues:(1) Whether there is a support judgment, order, or payment schedule on arrearages or reimbursement.(2) Whether the petitioner is the obligor covered by the support judgment or order.(3) Whether the support obligor is or is not in compliance with the judgment or order of support."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (k)(1)-(3), scope of judicial review (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=17520.)
  Known gap: This clause states the 20-calendar-day hearing requirement and the first three of the four review issues the statute lists (a fourth issue, the extent to which an obligor's needs warrant a conditional release, is described in subdivision (k)(4) but is not quoted in this clause's citation); it does not restate the separate seven-calendar-day service requirement on the local child support agency or the court's authority to uphold, unconditionally release, or conditionally release the license.

THIS PROCESS IS THE SOLE ADMINISTRATIVE REMEDY, AND THE APA DOES NOT APPLY
Under California law, the review process described in subdivision (h) of Family Code Section 17520 -- the written request for review to the local child support agency -- constitutes the sole administrative remedy for contesting the issuance of a temporary license or the denial or suspension of a license under this statute. The statute expressly states that the Administrative Procedure Act's administrative adjudication provisions do not apply to a denial, suspension, failure to issue or renew a license, or issuance of a temporary license made under Section 17520.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The process described in subdivision (h) shall constitute the sole administrative remedy for contesting the issuance of a temporary license or the denial or suspension of a license under this section. The procedures specified in the administrative adjudication provisions of the Administrative Procedure Act (Chapter 4.5 (commencing with Section 11400) and Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 11500) of Part 1 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code) shall not apply to the denial, suspension, or failure to issue or renew a license or the issuance of a temporary license pursuant to this section."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (o), sole administrative remedy and APA inapplicability (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=17520.)
  Known gap: This clause states only that the Section 17520 review process is the exclusive administrative remedy and that the Administrative Procedure Act's adjudication provisions do not apply; it does not address whether or how a party might separately pursue judicial remedies outside the review-and-judicial-review process this statute itself creates (addressed in a separate clause of this document), and it does not independently verify the scope of the referenced Administrative Procedure Act provisions.

SPECIFIC PROTECTIONS FOR A SUSPENDED DRIVER'S LICENSE
Under California law, when a driver's license, including a commercial driver's license, is suspended or revoked under Family Code Section 17520, the statute states that the suspension or revocation does not subject the licensee to vehicle impoundment under Vehicle Code Section 14602.6, and does not subject the licensee to increased vehicle liability insurance costs.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The suspension or revocation of a driver’s license, including a commercial driver’s license, under this section shall not subject the licensee to vehicle impoundment pursuant to Section 14602.6 of the Vehicle Code.(2) Notwithstanding any other law, the suspension or revocation of a driver’s license, including a commercial driver’s license, under this section shall not subject the licensee to increased costs for vehicle liability insurance."
  — Cal. Fam. Code Section 17520 (California Legislative Information text), subdivision (w)(1)-(2), no impoundment and no increased insurance cost (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=17520.)
  Known gap: This clause states only these two specific driver's-license protections created by subdivision (w); it does not address whether other consequences of a driver's license suspension under different statutes (for example, unrelated to Section 17520) would still apply, and it does not independently verify Vehicle Code Section 14602.6's own impoundment provisions.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT -- NOT A CERTIFICATION, RELEASE, OR COURT ORDER
I, Taylor Morgan, and I, Jordan Alex Lee, each acknowledge that I have reviewed this information sheet describing California's child support license suspension and denial program under Family Code Section 17520, in connection with case number CGC-26-123456 pending in Sacramento County, involving a license described as: California driver's license (Department of Motor Vehicles), with arrears (if any) of $4,800 as of September 1, 2026.

Executed on September 6, 2026.

☐ _________________________ Taylor Morgan, signature

☐ _________________________ Jordan Alex Lee, signature

Sacramento, California

[This information sheet is prepared for use alongside an actual filing or proceeding in the appropriate California superior court or before the appropriate local child support agency. It does not itself certify any obligor to the Department of Child Support Services or any board, request or grant any temporary license, release, suspension, or judicial review, and it does not create any attorney-client relationship or privilege. Only the local child support agency, the applicable licensing board, and the applicable superior court determine what actually occurs in a specific case, and this is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney.]
